Recruitment Process Outsourcing is a strategic hiring model where an organization transfers part or all of its recruitment function to an external specialist provider . Unlike a traditional agency filling a single vacancy , an RPO partner embeds itself into the organization's talent acquisition structure , managing everything from workforce planning and candidate sourcing to recruitment technology and hiring analytics . "An RPO partner doesn't just fill roles — it becomes an integrated extension of your internal talent acquisition function, owning the end-to-end recruitment process ." 💡 What Makes RPO Different: A traditional staffing agency fills individual roles on demand. An RPO provider , by contrast, takes ownership of the entire recruitment function — from strategy and sourcing to technology and reporting — operating as a true extension of your HR team. Recruitment models differ based on integration depth and hiring needs: Traditional agency – Provides low integration for single vacancies and one-off hiring needs. RPO provider – Offers high integration by acting as an embedded recruitment partner for scalable hiring. In-house recruiting – Provides full internal control, best suited for large and stable HR teams. 🔑 Key Takeaway: RPO is not a quick-fix staffing solution — it's a long-term talent acquisition partnership designed to deliver scalable, data-driven hiring aligned with your business growth strategy . How RPO differs from simply hiring a recruiter Recruitment becomes hard to manage as companies grow, not because teams underperform, but because the process wasn't designed for scale. An RPO provider handles operational work: CV screening, interview coordination, employer branding, and sourcing strategy. Internal HR teams focus on people decisions rather than process logistics. The scope can be total, covering the full recruitment lifecycle , or selective, outsourcing only high-friction areas like candidate sourcing or recruitment marketing while keeping hiring decisions in-house. What happens when hiring volume outgrows your current stack? Most teams manage recruitment complexity using multiple tools: an applicant tracking system, a sourcing platform, and spreadsheets. This approach breaks down as hiring volume increases or the organization expands across different entities and countries. Platforms like Cercli consolidate hiring, HR, and payroll into a single AI-native system, enabling teams to manage multi-entity, multi-country workforces without the fragmentation that drives outsourcing decisions. What RPO providers actually do day-to-day According to Global Market Insights Inc. , the global recruitment outsourcing market was worth approximately USD 11 billion in 2025. RPO providers offer recruitment expertise, sourcing tools, employer branding support, and reporting capabilities that internal teams lack time to develop. Services include workforce planning, passive candidate sourcing, structured interview coordination, and recruitment analytics tracking time-to-hire, cost-per-hire, and pipeline conversion rates. When does RPO actually make sense? RPO makes the most sense when an organization faces a genuine capacity gap it cannot close through process improvement alone. Rapid business expansion into new markets, large-scale seasonal hiring, or building a recruitment function in a country where the team has no local sourcing knowledge are legitimate use cases. RPO is not well-suited for compensating for disconnected internal systems, since outsourcing does not fix underlying data fragmentation or reporting gaps that made recruitment feel broken in the first place. The Global Market Insights Inc. report projects that the recruitment outsourcing market will reach USD 25.8 billion by 2034, reflecting growing demand and the trend of many organizations choosing to pay for external capacity rather than build internal capability. This choice warrants careful examination before signing an engagement. The harder question is whether the benefits outweigh the costs upon closer examination. Benefits and Challenges of Recruitment Process Outsourcing RPO can reduce cost-per-hire by up to 50% and improve time-to-fill by up to 40% , according to Hueman RPO — critical advantages when competing for top candidates. These results depend on a well-structured engagement , a provider who understands your business , and internal oversight to make changes when needed. "RPO can reduce cost-per-hire by up to 50% and improve time-to-fill by up to 40% ." — Hueman RPO Modern recruitment platforms improve hiring efficiency and reduce costs: Cost-per-hire reduction – Can deliver up to 50% savings on recruitment costs. Time-to-fill improvement – Can make hiring processes up to 40% faster. Competitive candidate access – Provides significantly improved access to qualified talent. 🎯 Key Point: RPO's biggest advantages — lower costs and faster hiring — are only realized when paired with a well-structured engagement and active internal oversight . 💡 Tip: Before signing with an RPO provider, always confirm they have deep knowledge of your industry — a generic approach will dilute these measurable gains . Where RPO creates the most value The clearest wins come from scale and specialization. When a business enters a new market, launches a major project, or needs to hire fifty engineers in six months, an RPO provider can handle that volume without permanently expanding the internal team. Providers bring structured hiring workflows , sourcing infrastructure, and specialist recruiters with networks in hard-to-fill disciplines: expertise that lean HR teams stretched across multiple geographies struggle to replicate internally. What do reduced oversight and brand consistency risks look like in practice? The challenges are real, though less dramatic than critics suggest. Reduced direct oversight most often emerges when an external team manages candidate communication, sourcing decisions, and pipeline activity; misalignment can accumulate quietly. Employer brand consistency is a related pressure—if recruiters representing your organization don't speak your culture fluently, candidates notice, and first impressions in hiring are nearly impossible to reverse. Cultural onboarding for an RPO partner requires time, an investment easy to underestimate at contract stage. Can consolidating tools remove the operational chaos that makes outsourcing feel necessary? Most teams handle recruitment complexity with multiple tools: an applicant tracking system, a sourcing platform, a shared spreadsheet for offer tracking. This works until hiring volume increases or compliance requirements multiply across jurisdictions. That fragmentation often makes RPO feel necessary. Platforms like Cercli address the underlying problem directly, consolidating hiring, HR, and payroll into a single AI-native system built for multi-entity, multi-country teams, eliminating the operational chaos that drives outsourcing decisions. Does the cost of RPO actually justify itself? RPO is not cheap, and returns depend heavily on volume and engagement length. Organizations with stable, predictable hiring needs may find that the fixed cost of a managed service outweighs savings, especially if an internal team could achieve similar outcomes with better tooling and clearer processes. Data privacy adds another layer of consideration. Sharing candidate information with an external provider requires strict contractual governance, particularly for employers operating across jurisdictions with distinct data protection frameworks. Getting that wrong is both a compliance risk and a trust risk with candidates already cautious about where their information goes. When does RPO work best as a strategic choice? RPO works best as a strategic extension of an existing talent acquisition function , not as a replacement for one. A well-chosen provider strengthens a solid internal foundation, whereas outsourcing a fragmented one merely addresses symptoms while leaving root causes unresolved. How those trade-offs play out depends heavily on where you are hiring , and context changes everything. Each country has different labor laws , visa sponsorship rules , contract requirements , and statutory benefits . title: People with Disabilities, Advocates Sue City of Portland and Multnomah County Over Inaccessible Emergency Systems
summary: Federal lawsuit follows 2021 heat wave that killed 69 people and years of ignored warnings from the city's auditor
body_text: People with Disabilities, Advocates Sue City of Portland and Multnomah County Over Inaccessible Emergency Systems Federal lawsuit follows 2021 heat wave that killed 69 people and years of ignored warnings from the city's auditor Case : Simeone v. Multnomah County Affiliate : ACLU of Oregon July 29, 2026 9:00 am ACLU Affiliate ACLU of Oregon Spokesperson Malhar Shah › ACLU Disability Rights Program Media Contact media@aclu.org (212) 549-2666 125 Broad Street 18th Floor New York, NY 10004 United States PORTLAND, Ore. — People with disabilities and disability rights advocates have filed a federal lawsuit against the city of Portland, Multnomah County, and their top elected officials, alleging that the jurisdictions' emergency management systems fail to protect people with disabilities before, during, and after disasters — in violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, and Oregon law. “Five years ago, as temperatures soared above 115 degrees, far too many disabled Portland residents could not reach cooling centers or even access usable emergency information. As a result, people with disabilities were overrepresented among those who died,” said Malhar Shah, senior staff attorney with the ACLU Disability Rights Program . “With the threat of extreme weather and disasters like wildfires only accelerating, Portland and Multnomah County have a legal duty to make their emergency system accessible to people with disabilities and give them the equal opportunity to survive.” The complaint seeks to avoid a repetition of the city of Portland and Multnomah County's response to the June 2021 extreme heat wave, when temperatures reached an all-time high of 116 degrees and 69 people died of heat-related causes in Multnomah County — with people with disabilities overrepresented among the dead . Many victims lived on upper floors of multi-family housing, in trailers and RVs, or were unhoused. Survivors with disabilities reported being unable to reach cooling centers, obtain accessible transportation, or access timely, usable emergency information. That risk is not abstract. A local wildfire expert who studied the 2025 Eaton Fire in Los Angeles — which killed at least 17 people and destroyed 9,000 structures — found that Portland is less prepared and has fewer resources than Los Angeles did before that disaster . Forest Park has only two wildfire-detection cameras, and Southeast Portland's Oaks Bottom area, where three fires have already ignited this year, has none at all . “ We’re in a wildfire emergency right now statewide and people with disabilities cannot be an afterthought,” said Jake Cornett, executive director at Disability Rights Oregon . “We often hear about victims with disabilities in the aftermath of disasters — and that’s not good enough. We need the city and county to have an inclusive plan to evacuate and shelter people with disabilities long before a wildfire, flood, earthquake, or some other disaster strikes.” The lawsuit was filed by Disability Rights Oregon, Disability Law United, the American Civil Liberties Union, and law firm Cambreleng & Marton, and names the City of Portland, Multnomah County, Portland Mayor Keith Wilson, and Multnomah County Board Chair Jessica Vega Pederson as defendants. Plaintiffs in the lawsuit are Disability Rights Oregon, Oregon’s federally designated protection and advocacy organization, and Bridges Oregon, a nonprofit that serves Deaf, DeafBlind, Hard of Hearing, and Late-Deafened Oregonians. Three individuals also join the case: Audra Pearson , a Portland resident with cerebral palsy who relies on a powered wheelchair, paratransit, and round-the-clock caregiver support: “I can't just grab a bag and walk out the door during an emergency — I need an accessible vehicle, a shelter that fits my wheelchair, and staff who know how to help me. Nobody has ever asked what I'd need to survive a disaster, even though it's obvious I'd need help. That has to change before it costs someone their life." Jonathan Simeone , a Portland homeowner who is blind: “Learning about the emergency system created and maintained by Portland and Multnomah County, I realized they do not include those of us with disabilities in their emergency planning and that their violations of our civil rights have resulted in those of us with disabilities being more likely to suffer injury or death during an emergency simply because we are disabled and Portland and Multnomah County have not considered the rights of disabled people with the care they have considered the rights of nondisabled people." Philip Wolfe , a Deaf Portland resident: "I have the same right to survive a disaster as anyone else, but every time there’s a wildfire, heat wave, or other dangerous emergency, I worry whether I'll get the information I need in time.” The lawsuit alleges that Portland and Multnomah County's emergency system denies people with disabilities meaningful access at every phase of disaster response: Alerts and warnings are shared in inaccessible formats, including maps without descriptive text and social media videos without captions or ASL interpretation. Evacuation assistance is unreliable: the city and county have no adequate way to identify residents who need help, lack accessible vehicles and trained drivers, and exclude entire categories of residents with disabilities — including people in high-rises, psychiatric facilities, and group homes — from evacuation plans altogether. Shelters and recovery centers are riddled with known accessibility barriers, and there is no concrete plan to fix them or to ensure access to medication and equipment after a disaster. Planning, training, and outreach continue to exclude the disability community, despite years of advocacy and documented requests to be included. “This isn't a case of a government caught off guard,” said Ayelet Weiss at Disability Law United . “The City's own auditor and community members have urged the Defendants to include individuals with disabilities in a comprehensive planning process for years. That hasn't happened, and the needs of the disabled go unaddressed. As the City Auditor put it , ‘This lack of preparation puts the lives of people with disabilities at risk.’” The lawsuit asks the court to declare that Portland and Multnomah County's emergency planning, preparedness, response, and recovery programs violate the ADA, Section 504, and Oregon law; order the city and county to design, implement, and maintain an emergency management system — covering alerts, evacuation, shelter, and planning — that is fully accessible to people with disabilities; and award damages to individual plaintiffs and reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs to organizational plaintiffs. “When the law is ignored for years, litigation is the necessary next step to ensure equal protection for all Oregonians,” said Rebecca Cambreleng, partner at Cambreleng & Marton and co-counsel on the case . “We intend to see this through until the city and county meet their legal obligations to everyone with disabilities.” Plaintiffs tried to resolve these issues without litigation by notifying the city and county of their findings in February 2025 and meeting with counsel in March 2026. After those efforts failed to produce meaningful commitments, plaintiffs notified defendants of intent to sue in June 2026. The complaint is available here: https://www.aclu.org/cases/simeone-v-multnomah-county?document=Complaint Oregon Jul 2026 Disability Rights Simeone v. Press Release Jun 2026 Disability Rights ACLU Statement on DOJ Memo Threatening the Right to Community Living for People with Disabilities WASHINGTON – The Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) has issued a memorandum that incorrectly purports that neither federal disability rights laws nor Supreme Court precedent enshrine the right of people with disabilities to live integrated lives in their communities, instead of being segregated in institutions. Zoe Brennan-Krohn, director of the Disability Rights Program at the American Civil Liberties Union, had the following response: “Trump’s Justice Department cannot erase federal laws and decades of legal precedent with a single opinion. The memo itself acknowledges it is ‘out of step’ with longstanding and consistent federal court opinion interpreting what the Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act require, but it is far worse than that. This is a blatant attempt to undermine the rights of disabled people. “Nearly three decades ago, the Supreme Court in Olmstead v. L.C. recognized a ‘right to live in the world,’ and also recognized that state and local governments have an obligation to end the long and dark history of segregation and institutionalization of disabled people. Olmstead confirmed that disability rights laws require states to provide people with disabilities with services in an integrated manner in the communities. For far too long, disabled people faced neglect, isolation, and inhumane conditions in institutions. Olmstead made clear that this segregation must end. “The DOJ’s statement is wrong on the law, and does not change the rights of disabled people. The right to live in the community is foundational to disability rights law. We won’t stop fighting to protect it.” Aclu Statement On Doj Memo Threatening The Right To Community Living For People With Disabilities. Explore Press Release. title: Jersey Ready for the world: How PSE&G helped power the FIFA World Cup
summary: See how PSE&G helped power the FIFA World Cup at MetLife Stadium through two years of planning, infrastructure investments and reliable energy service.
body_text: Supporting one of the world’s biggest sporting events took years of planning, coordination and teamwork. From inspecting and maintaining equipment that serves MetLife Stadium and surrounding event locations to monitoring our systems and staying ready to respond, every effort reflected the teamwork, pride and dedication our employees bring to their work every day. Click below to meet some of the PSE&G employees and partners whose planning, preparation and teamwork helped make New Jersey ready for the FIFA World Cup Final. When the final whistle blew at MetLife Stadium , the world celebrated an unforgettable FIFA World Cup. More than 2 billion people watched as Spain lifted the trophy before a sold-out crowd in East Rutherford ,￼ while countless fans gathered at Fan Fests and watch parties across the region. For us, the successful conclusion of the tournament demonstrated that years of planning, collaboration and preparation had achieved exactly what they were designed to do—we were Jersey Ready for the World. While fans focused on the action on the field, our employees quietly delivered what they always strive to provide — safe, reliable energy when it mattered most. We’ve powered New Jersey for more than 120 years , providing reliable electric service to 2.4 million customers and natural gas service to 1.9 million customers. Preparing for an event of this magnitude wasn’t something that began on game day. It was the result of decades of investments as part of our ongoing efforts to strengthen and modernize our energy system, combined with more than two years of focused planning that began in February 2024. That preparation included: Approximately 100 employees representing gas and electric operations, emergency preparedness, physical and cybersecurity, information technology and more working together across the company. Close coordination with the stadium and its partners, state and local public safety agencies, New Jersey law enforcement and regional partners. Ongoing electric and gas inspections, infrastructure hardening, emergency preparedness drills as well as practice game-day scenarios and simulations. Inspection and monitoring of dozens of electric circuits and gas facilities supporting critical World Cup infrastructure throughout the region. Strategically positioned field personnel, multiple contingency plans and around-the-clock operational support throughout the tournament. The outcome was eight FIFA World Cup matches hosted at MetLife Stadium — including the championship — completed safely and without disruption. Inside our operations center, teams monitored the energy system in real time while field crews stood ready to respond if needed. Fortunately, thanks to the extensive preparation and coordination that had taken place over the previous two years, they were never called upon to respond to a major incident. That’s what being Jersey Ready means — anticipating challenges before they happen, preparing for every possibility and delivering reliable service when it matters most. While the World Cup may only last a short time, our mission remains the same: keeping our customers and communities safely connected, whether we’re responding to severe storms , weathering extreme temperatures or supporting a global event watched by billions. title: Employee Verification for Small Businesses and Startups in India
summary: Learn why employee verification is essential for small businesses. Prevent costly hiring mistakes with PAN, UAN, Voter ID, and DL verification.
body_text: Insights & Resources Employee Verification for Small Businesses and Startups in India July 28, 2026 Shashank Yadav No comments yet Why Small Businesses Need Verification More Than Corporates Do There is a common misconception that employee background verification is a “big company thing” — something that MNCs and banks do because they have compliance departments and HR budgets. Small businesses and startups, the thinking goes, hire people they know, or people who come through trusted referrals, and that is good enough. This thinking is dangerously wrong. Here is why small businesses are actually more vulnerable to bad hires than large corporations: The financial impact is proportionally devastating. A bad hire that costs Rs 10 lakh is an inconvenience for a company with Rs 500 crore in revenue. For a startup with Rs 50 lakh in annual revenue, the same bad hire is an existential crisis — 20 percent of the entire year’s revenue gone. There is no safety net. Large companies have legal departments, compliance teams, and insurance policies to mitigate the damage from a fraudulent employee. A small business owner typically bears the entire burden — financial, legal, and operational — personally. Small teams amplify the damage. In a team of 10 people, one bad hire represents 10 percent of the workforce. Their incompetence, dishonesty, or misconduct affects every colleague, every project, and every client interaction. In a large organisation of 10,000 employees, one bad hire is a rounding error. Referrals are not verification. Many small business owners hire through personal networks and treat a referral as a substitute for verification. But the person making the referral may not know the candidate’s full history. They may not know about a fabricated degree, a concealed termination, or a pending court case. Trust is not a verification method. Informal hiring processes create legal exposure. Under the DPDP Act 2023, all employers — regardless of size — face the same data protection obligations. If a small business hires someone without basic identity verification and that person commits fraud or causes a data breach, the business has no defensible documentation to show it exercised reasonable care. What Does a Bad Hire Actually Cost a Small Business? Let us break down the numbers for a typical Indian small business — a retail store, restaurant, logistics company, or professional services firm with 10 to 50 employees: Scenario: You hire a store manager at Rs 30,000 per month. Three months later, you discover they fabricated their previous employment and have no actual management experience. During those three months: You paid Rs 90,000 in salary and benefits for substandard work. You spent Rs 30,000 to Rs 50,000 on recruitment (job posting, interviews, onboarding). The store’s performance declined — conservatively, Rs 1,00,000 in lost revenue due to poor management. You now need to recruit and train a replacement, costing another Rs 50,000 to Rs 1,00,000. If the fraudulent manager mishandled cash or inventory, add those direct losses. If they damaged client relationships, the long-term revenue impact could be several times higher. Total cost: Rs 3 lakh to Rs 5 lakh — for a single hire at Rs 30,000 per month. Now compare that to the cost of identity verification: under Rs 500 per candidate for all four checks. The return on investment is not 10x or 50x — it is effectively infinite, because you are preventing a loss that could sink the business. Which Verification Checks Should Small Businesses Prioritise? You do not need to run every type of background check for every hire. Here is a practical prioritisation framework for small businesses with limited budgets: Essential for Every Hire: Identity Verification PAN check: Confirms the candidate’s tax identity and legal name. Takes seconds and costs under Rs 100. This is the single most important check because it confirms the person’s identity against the Income Tax Department database, which is extremely difficult to fake. UAN check: Reveals the candidate’s actual employment history through PF records. If they claim to have worked at three companies over the past five years, the UAN will show whether PF contributions were actually received from those employers. This is the most cost-effective way to verify employment claims without contacting previous employers individually. Strongly Recommended: Secondary Identity Cross-Reference Voter ID check: Provides an independent identity verification from the Election Commission database. Cross-referencing the name and date of birth from the Voter ID against the PAN record gives you high confidence in the candidate’s identity. Driving Licence check: Essential for any role involving driving, delivery, or field work. Also useful as a third identity cross-reference for all roles. When to Invest in Full Background Checks For most small business hires — shop staff, delivery executives, administrative assistants, junior team members — identity verification across PAN, Voter ID, DL, and UAN provides sufficient due diligence. Consider investing in full background checks (education verification, criminal records, address verification) for roles that involve handling cash or financial transactions, access to sensitive customer or business data, managing other employees, representing the company externally in sales or partnerships, and any senior or leadership position. How to Verify Employees Under Rs 500 Per Candidate Here is the step-by-step process for running affordable identity verification: Step 1: Choose a Self-Serve Digital Platform The key to keeping costs low is using a self-serve platform that lets you run checks directly, without a BGV agency acting as a middleman. Traditional agencies charge Rs 2,000 to Rs 8,000 per candidate because they bundle checks with account management, reporting dashboards, and enterprise features that small businesses do not need. A self-serve platform like ID Verify by SalaryBox gives you direct access to the same government database checks at a fraction of the cost. Step 2: Run All Four Checks in a Single Flow Instead of verifying documents one at a time through separate portals, use a platform that bundles PAN, Voter ID, Driving Licence, and UAN checks into a single candidate flow. This saves time and reduces the chance of overlooking a check. Step 3: Review the Cross-Record Analysis The most valuable insight from running multiple checks is not any single result — it is the comparison across records. When names, dates of birth, and other identity details agree across PAN, Voter ID, DL, and UAN records, you have strong confidence in the candidate’s identity. When they conflict, you have an immediate red flag worth investigating. Step 4: Download and File the Report Generate a PDF report of the verification results. Store it in the candidate’s file — whether that is a physical folder, a shared drive, or your HR platform. This report serves as evidence that you exercised due diligence, which protects you legally if issues arise later. Common Mistakes Small Businesses Make with Employee Verification Mistake 1: Verifying Only After a Problem Occurs Many small business owners only think about verification after they have already been burned by a bad hire. By then, the damage is done. Verification is a preventive measure, not a reactive one. Build it into your standard hiring process so every candidate goes through the same checks before receiving an offer. Mistake 2: Relying on Photocopies Instead of Database Checks Asking candidates to submit photocopies of their PAN card, Aadhaar, or Voter ID and then visually inspecting these documents is not verification. Sophisticated fakes can pass visual inspection easily. Real verification means querying the actual government database to confirm that the document details match official records. Mistake 3: Skipping Verification for “Trusted” Referrals A referral from a friend, family member, or business associate is valuable context, but it is not a substitute for verification. The referrer may not know the candidate’s full history. They may not know about a forged degree, a concealed termination, or a financial fraud at a previous employer. Verify every hire, regardless of the source. Mistake 4: Assuming Verification Is Too Expensive This was true a decade ago when the only option was hiring a BGV agency. Today, digital identity verification costs under Rs 500 per candidate — less than a team lunch. The cost of not verifying (Rs 3 lakh to Rs 50 lakh per bad hire) makes verification one of the highest-ROI investments a small business can make. Mistake 5: Not Storing Verification Records Running checks but not saving the results defeats half the purpose. If a verified employee later causes a problem and you have no documentation of the verification, you lose the legal protection that verification provides. Always download and file the verification report. How ID Verify by SalaryBox Is Built for Small Teams ID Verify by SalaryBox was designed with Indian small businesses and startups in mind. Every design decision — from the workflow to the pricing — reflects the reality of how small teams hire. No setup required. No implementation project, no API integration, no demo call with a sales team. Create an account at verify.salarybox.in and run your first check in minutes. All checks in one flow. Run PAN, Voter ID, Driving Licence, and UAN checks from a single candidate flow. No switching between tools, no managing multiple vendor accounts. Cross-record comparison. ID Verify automatically flags when identity details disagree across records. You do not need HR expertise to spot discrepancies — the platform does the analysis for you. Pay per check. No monthly subscriptions, no annual contracts, no minimum volumes. You pay only when you run a check. If you hire three people this month and zero next month, you pay for three checks and nothing more. Clear PDF reports. Every verification generates a downloadable report that your hiring manager can review and your records can store. Professional-grade documentation without enterprise-grade complexity. Secure by default. Sensitive identity data is masked until payment is complete. Your verification history is private to your account. Data is handled responsibly at every step. Start your first verification at verify.salarybox.in Frequently Asked Questions Is employee verification legally mandatory for small businesses in India? There is no single law mandating background verification for all private employers. However, the DPDP Act 2023 requires all employers to handle employee data responsibly, and several industries (BFSI, IT/ITES) have sector-specific verification requirements. Even where not legally mandated, verification protects small businesses from negligent hiring claims and provides documentation of due diligence. I only hire 2 to 3 people a year. Is verification still worth it? Absolutely. In fact, the lower your hiring volume, the more each hire matters. If you hire 3 people a year and one turns out to be fraudulent, that is a 33 percent failure rate. Spending Rs 500 per candidate (Rs 1,500 total per year) to prevent a potential loss of Rs 3 lakh to Rs 5 lakh is one of the best investments you can make. Can I verify candidates myself without an HR department? Yes. Self-serve platforms like ID Verify by SalaryBox are designed for exactly this use case. You do not need HR expertise, technical knowledge, or a compliance team. Enter the candidate’s details, select the checks, review the results, and download the report. How long does the verification process take? Digital identity verification returns results in minutes. You can run a candidate through all four checks (PAN, Voter ID, DL, UAN) and have a downloadable report within a single sitting. This is in contrast to traditional BGV agencies, which typically take 7 to 21 business days. What if a candidate refuses to be verified? Under the DPDP Act 2023, candidates have the right to refuse consent for verification. However, you are equally within your rights to make successful identity verification a condition of employment. If a candidate refuses basic identity checks, consider that a significant red flag — legitimate candidates with nothing to hide rarely object to verification. Do I need different verification for different types of employees? For most small business hires (shop staff, delivery executives, office assistants, junior team members), identity verification across PAN, Voter ID, DL, and UAN provides strong baseline due diligence. For roles involving financial responsibility, access to sensitive data, or management authority, consider adding education verification and criminal record checks through a full background verification service. Can I use ID Verify for contract workers and freelancers? Yes. ID Verify works for any individual you need to verify, whether they are full-time employees, contract workers, freelancers, or temporary staff. The self-serve, pay-per-check model makes it practical to verify even short-term engagements. Related Shashank Yadav Leave a Reply Cancel reply

title: How to Create AI Judge Metrics You Can Trust
summary: How to use human review in Coval to calibrate your LLM-as-a-judge metrics: label conversations, check agreement, read disagreements, fix the prompt, and re-test.
body_text: How to use human review in Coval to calibrate your LLM-as-a-judge metrics. If you evaluate an AI agent at any real scale, an LLM judge is scoring your conversations. It reads each transcript and answers questions like “Did the agent resolve the issue?” across thousands of calls, far faster than any human could. But how do you know the judge itself is right? Human review answers that. Your QA team can label a small sample of conversations yourself, see where the LLM judge is wrong, fix the metric, and verify the fix. The loop looks like this: The calibration loop ↻ repeat until you trust the judge 1 Label conversations 2 Check the agreement rate 3 Read the disagreements 4 Fix the metric prompt 5 Re-test the same calls 1 Label conversations Open a run and, for a sample of calls, agree or disagree with the judge. Each label becomes ground truth. 2 Check the agreement rate See how often the judge's verdicts matched your labels. High agreement means it reads calls the way you do. 3 Read the disagreements Inspect the rows where the judge and the humans split — the highest-signal screen, because disagreements cluster around a pattern. 4 Fix the metric prompt Teach the judge the edge case the humans found. Usually a sentence or two — no model change, no agent change. 5 Re-test the same calls Re-run the new judge on the same labeled calls and watch the disagreements flip. Then repeat until you trust it. The calibration loop — click any step. Label, check agreement, read disagreements, fix the prompt, re-test, repeat. Let’s walk the loop with one real metric. A team running an outbound voice agent had a compliance check: did the agent disclose that it’s an AI during the call? In regulated industries, skipping that disclosure is a legal problem. The metric kept failing calls, and it wasn’t clear why. Here’s how human review got to the bottom of it. Step 1: Label some conversations Open any run and you’ll see the transcript next to every metric that ran on it, each with the judge’s verdict. Your job: agree or disagree. Pick Yes, No, or N/A, and add a short note saying why. Our team read the failed disclosure calls and started overruling the judge, with notes like “agent doesn’t have the chance to verify” and “conversation ended early.” Each label is now ground truth. Try it — agree or disagree with the judge Factual Accuracy AI Judge Yes Human Review YesNoN/A ✓ you agree with the judge ● disagreement saved as ground truth marked not applicable Identity Verification Flow AI Judge Yes Human Review YesNoN/A ✓ you agree with the judge ● disagreement saved as ground truth marked not applicable FDCPA: No Misleading Claims AI Judge Yes Human Review YesNoN/A ✓ you agree with the judge ● disagreement saved as ground truth marked not applicable Identity & Purpose Disclosure AI Judge Yes Human Review YesNoN/A ✓ you agree with the judge ● disagreement saved as ground truth marked not applicable Escalation Handling AI Judge Yes Human Review YesNoN/A ✓ you agree with the judge ● disagreement saved as ground truth marked not applicable Step 1 in Coval: every metric shows the AI judge’s verdict beside a Human Review control. Agree or disagree, and each label becomes ground truth. (This one’s interactive — click around.) Labeling as a team? Create a Human Review project. It gives reviewers a shared queue, tracks progress, and can auto-add new conversations. Link Step 2: Check the agreement rate Now open the metric on the Metrics page. The agreement rate shows how often the judge’s verdicts matched your labels. For our disclosure metric: 89% agreement across 314 conversations, with 35 disagreements. The metric page: 89% agreement, 279 agreements, 35 disagreements. High agreement means the judge sees calls the way you do. Low agreement means the judge is misreading calls, or your metric prompt is too ambiguous for even you to answer consistently. Either way, you want to know. Step 3: Read the disagreements Click into the annotations and look at the rows where the judge and the humans split. This is the highest-signal screen in the workflow, because disagreements cluster around a pattern. Disagreement rows: the judge said No, the reviewer said Yes, with reasoning on both sides. Ours did. In every disputed call, a wrong party picked up or the caller hung up early. The agent never confirmed who it was talking to, so it correctly never disclosed anything. The judge didn’t know that ending was legitimate, so it failed the agent for skipping a step the call never reached. The agent wasn’t broken. The metric was. Disagreements cut both ways. Sometimes the judge is right and the label is wrong. Correct the label, and your ground truth gets stronger. Step 4: Fix the metric prompt The fix was one paragraph added to the judge’s prompt: if the caller is a wrong party or the call ends before identity verification, the agent may never reach the disclosure stage. In that case, answer Yes. No model change. No agent change. The fix, live in the prompt: the “Note:” paragraph teaches the judge the edge case the humans found. Step 5: Re-test on the same conversations After editing the prompt, click Test Metric . Coval runs the new judge against the same conversations you already labeled and shows whether the disagreements flip. The calls our judge had been failing came back as passes, matching the human labels. Old results stay as history, and the improved prompt now scores every future run. You can even see the fix in the judge’s own reasoning afterward: “identity was confirmed but debt details were not disclosed, so the answer is YES per instructions.” The judge learned the boundary the humans drew for it. Want Claude to run the analysis for you? Coval ships a Claude Code skill that does steps 2 through 4 automatically: it pulls your labels and the judge’s reasoning, calculates agreement, finds the disagreement patterns, and proposes an improved metric prompt. You stay in the loop, since nothing changes without your approval. Get the skill on GitHub Why this is important In this team’s case, most of what looked like agent failures traced back to how the metric was written. Without human review, they would have spent weeks fixing an agent that was already behaving correctly. That’s the real payoff. Calibrated metrics mean your dashboard says what it means, so when you change your agent and the numbers move, you can believe them. And you don’t label forever: as agreement climbs, you review less and trust the judge more. Start small. Pick your most important metric, label twenty or thirty conversations, and open the agreement rate. Whatever you find, you’ll know something about your evals you didn’t know this morning. Don’t want to label yourself? Coval offers labeling as a service: trained human reviewers who label your conversations and calibrate your metrics for you. Reach out to brooke@coval.dev .

title: The Firewatcher
summary: The Firewatcher is our first-responder for issues that may impact our partners. If there’s an incident, they coordinate the response. Every engineer at Gordian is trained to be on Firewatch, and each of us takes on week-long shifts.
body_text: From the lookout station, the Firewatcher scans the horizon. In the distance, they see something so subtle that most would miss - a small, rising plume of smoke against the clouds. With their compass, map and alidade, they quickly calculate the smoke’s location and relay it to fire suppression teams. ‍ At Gordian, we also have a Firewatcher. They’re on constant lookout for potential problems among the hundreds of services we’ve integrated. Instead of maps and alidades, they use comprehensive monitoring and alerting tools that track every part of our system. At any given second, our systems are processing critical transactions. From purchasing bags to securing the last seat on an urgent flight home, our partners depend on these systems to serve their customers. ‍ The Firewatcher is our first-responder for issues that may impact our partners. If there’s an incident, they coordinate the response. Every engineer at Gordian is trained to be on Firewatch, and each of us takes on week-long shifts. ‍ Most of the time, Firewatch is quiet. Our systems hum along while handling tens-of-thousands of transactions. But every now and then, an airline we’ve integrated has an unexpected outage. When this happens, here’s how we respond. ‍ Smoke on the Horizon Like smoke against clouds, a few bad requests among thousands of successful ones could be easy to miss. However, our alerting systems are so sensitive that we often detect an airline outage before the airline themselves have even noticed the outage. Taking the role of Firewatcher, I will immediately begin pulling transaction traces using our custom-built logging and tracing tools. Analyzing these traces will allow me to quickly confirm the outage and determine its impact on our systems. ‍ Fire Suppression The next step would be mitigation. I will call in an additional engineer to assist with communications while asking others to remain on standby. The supporting engineer will contact the airline’s technical team directly and assist them in diagnosing the issue. While this is happening, I will notify our partners about the outage. While an airline outage is a critical issue, our systems are built to handle this and automatic failovers would already be taking place. This could include using alternate services or temporarily halting transactions with the problematic airline. We will quickly relay updates from the airline to our partners while keeping a close-eye on our systems. As the airline’s services come back up, we will see our alerts close and metrics gravitate to nominal levels. We then inform our partners that all services are back online. ‍ Reflection Once the incident has closed, we do what we call a “Reflection” every Friday. Here, I would create a detailed writeup, including a timeline and analysis of the incident. Our team would evaluate how we handled it and determine how we could further optimize our response. We may even throw-in hypothetical curveballs - what if there was a simultaneous outage in another service? - to test our ability to respond. We all document our ideas, which could include tuning alerts or building additional failovers, then assign them out to engineers to implement. The process of Reflection keeps us sharp and prepares us for situations regardless of whether we’ve seen them before. ‍ Impact Behind our systems and the hundreds of services we’ve integrated is the Firewatcher keeping a close and careful eye. They’re the first to spot a potential problem, the first to coordinate a response, and often the first point-of-contact for our partners. As a result, their actions have immediate impacts in ensuring our systems run smoothly. ‍ The Firewatcher is one of the most important roles at Gordian. Equipped with our monitoring and alerting tools, they’re ready to call-in a team and mobilize a response at even the most subtle sign of smoke.

title: How to train a small, highly performant model like Llama-3-8B?
summary: Third Party GenAI Risk Assessment, Monitoring, Detection and Mitigation. We enable you to detect unsanctioned AI tool use in real time, act based on controls and create internal audits for third party vendor risk.
body_text: Tl;Dr; Train on a large amount of high-quality data. Use LLMs to curate and filter data based on various quality metrics including toxicity (NSFW, abuse, harm, etc), deduplication, diversity, correctness, and style. With fine-tuning, an 8B param model can match the performance of GPT-4 for custom use cases at 1/50th of the cost. Why the 8B param model? Fits into 1 GPU. Cheaper and faster in training and inference. Optimize model performance Llama-3 was pre-trained on 15T tokens and fine-tuned on 10M tokens of high-quality data. Improving the size and quality of the dataset led to improvements in model performance. Llama-3-8B is comparable to Mixtral - a 4x larger model. The model showed continuous improvement with more pre-training tokens, even at 15T tokens - showing that there is room to get further improvements with more data, even for a 8B param model. Fine-Tuning Supervised fine-tuning of open-source models is already mainstream. An easy-to-adopt a modification of this is preference ranking - where a model is shown multiple, ranked outputs for a given prompt. This helps the model perform better in questions that it might previously have hallucinated on. Training of this kind improves the LLM's ability to pick the right answer given a prompt in the wild. Llama-3 used 10M human annotated samples for fine-tuning. Data Filtering using LLMs LLMs fine-tuned for data quality evaluation and filtering are used to further check and filter the data. This is essential at the large volumes of data as used by Llama-3. Data quality checks include: Correctness checks Style and form checks Context relevancy - ensuring that the response respects the context passed along with the query Filter abusive, harmful, NSFW data Using multiple LLMs to generate data eliminates bias in human-annotated datasets that lead to biased models. AI-Generated Data LLMs are used to generate high-quality question-answer pairs and instruction datasets for fine-tuning. The diversity of LLM-generated data can be maintained by applying algorithms like evol-instruct thereby reducing the problem of over-fitting on training data. AI Safety and Alignment Enforcing the responsible use of AI according to local laws is important to all enterprises. This includes the prevention of child pornography, leakage of PII, and prevention of AI use for violence, harassment, and self-harm. At the same time, for use cases like AI therapists and AI girlfriends, there is a need to ensure that the model is not censored and follows appropriate user instructions. Using synthetic data to simulate illegal behavior along with expected good behavior is essential to ensure the right model alignment for a specific use case.

title: What the Parkinson's Community Has Taught Me Over the Past Decade
body_text: What I remember most from those years is how hard people worked to stay close to the community. We saw how significant the unmet need was and how strongly the community wanted this part of Parkinson's to be taken seriously. We brought clinicians and advocates in. We held lunch-and-learns. We shared what we were hearing from the field. We wanted people inside the company to understand the environments families were dealing with every day, not just the science behind them. What Has Stayed with Me What I remember most from that period is relief. Not in a corporate sense. In a human one. I heard caregivers talk about the relief of finally having words for what they were seeing. I heard clinicians talk about the relief of having more direct conversations about symptoms that had too often gone unspoken. And I heard family members describe the moments when fear eased and connection returned. Those are not experiences you forget. I also saw how important the advocacy community was in that moment. Organizations were updating resources, answering questions, and helping families talk more openly about experiences that were still widely misunderstood. That partnership mattered then, and it still matters now. If there is one thing I hope more people understand during Parkinson's Disease Awareness Month, it is that Parkinson's is bigger than what most people can see. Families live with the visible symptoms, but they also live with the other things. The confusion. The fear. The changes that can affect how a person thinks, interprets the world, and relates to the people around them. Those experiences deserve more understanding and more honest conversation.
